title: Top 10 Essential Verbs in English, Part 3 (CEFR A0–A1 / A2)
dek: Master the third 10 high-frequency verbs in English: choose/buy/pay, remember/forget, feel, meet, decide (don't say 'decide a problem'), write/read/type, spend/waste, play (all variations), agree/disagree, and send/get. Conjugation tables on COSYtools.

blocks.text: Welcome to Part 3 of our core verb series for A0–A1 and A2 English learners! (Read [Part 1](top-10-verbs-en.html) and [Part 2](top-10-verbs-part-2-en.html) if you missed them). Here we cover 10 core decision-making, commerce, cognitive, social, and action verbs. All conjugation tables and verb forms are consultable on [COSYtools](https://cosylanguages.github.io/COSYtools/).
blocks.say: Welcome to Part 3 of our core verb series for A0–A1 and A2 English learners! (Read [Part 1](top-10-verbs-en.html) and [Part 2](top-10-verbs-part-2-en.html) if you missed them). Here we cover 10 core decision-making, commerce, cognitive, social, and action verbs. All conjugation tables and verb forms are consultable on [COSYtools](https://cosylanguages.github.io/COSYtools/).

blocks.text: Ten verbs are enough to shop, plan a meeting, share how you feel and send a message on your first day. <mark class="hl-handwritten">They are also the verbs where learners most often mix up the structure</mark>: pay for, decide on, agree with, play the. The good news is that the mistakes follow patterns, and patterns can be learned.
blocks.say: Ten verbs are enough to shop, plan a meeting, share how you feel and send a message on your first day. They are also the verbs where learners most often mix up the structure: pay for, decide on, agree with, play the. The good news is that the mistakes follow patterns, and patterns can be learned.

blocks.text: Read this article out loud. For each verb, start with the table and say the forms without looking. Then read the three sentences in the 'Say aloud' section, hide them, and repeat them from memory, changing one word to talk about your own life. Finish with the mistake card: it shows the sentence many beginners say, and the one to say instead. Speak first, understand the rule second: it is faster and more natural.

blocks.quote: You do not learn a verb until you can say it with a person, a place and a preposition.
blocks.say: You do not learn a verb until you can say it with a person, a place and a preposition.

rows: 'I choose a book', 'I buy groceries', 'I pay by card'.
'I remember your name', 'Don't forget your keys!'.
'remember to do', 'I forgot my password', 'hard to forget'.
'I feel happy', 'She feels cold', 'How do you feel?'.
'Nice to meet you', 'Let's meet at 5 PM', 'Meet my friend'.

'Play football / games', 'Play the guitar / piano', 'Play a role in a film'.
'play sports', 'play an instrument', 'play a key role'.

items:
**1. Choose / Buy / Pay:** Selection and commerce.
  • *Usage & Frames:* 'I choose a book', 'I buy groceries', 'I pay by card'.
  • *Useful Phrases:* 'choose wisely', 'buy online', 'pay attention', 'pay for dinner'.

**2. Remember / Forget:** Memory and cognition.
  • *Usage & Frames:* 'I remember your name', 'Don't forget your keys!'.
  • *Useful Phrases:* 'remember to do', 'I forgot my password', 'hard to forget'.

**3. Feel:** Physical and emotional state.
  • *Usage & Frames:* 'I feel happy', 'She feels cold', 'How do you feel?'.
  • *Useful Phrases:* 'feel like doing', 'feel well', 'feel tired'.

**4. Meet:** Social interactions and introductions.
  • *Usage & Frames:* 'Nice to meet you', 'Let's meet at 5 PM', 'Meet my friend'.
  • *Useful Phrases:* 'meet up', 'meet new people', 'pleased to meet you'.

**5. Decide:** Decision-making.
  • *Usage & Frames:* 'I decide to stay', 'Decide on a location'.
  • *Important Note:* We say 'solve/resolve a problem', NOT 'decide a problem'.
  • *Useful Phrases:* 'decide quickly', 'hard to decide', 'make up your mind'.

**6. Write / Read / Type:** Textual expression and literacy.
  • *Usage & Frames:* 'Write an email', 'Read a book', 'Type a message'.
  • *Useful Phrases:* 'write down', 'read aloud', 'type fast'.

**7. Spend / Waste:** Managing resources.
  • *Usage & Frames:* 'I spend money on books', 'Don't waste time!'.
  • *Useful Phrases:* 'spend time with family', 'waste energy', 'spend money on'.

**8. Play (all variations):** Games, sports, instruments, roles.
  • *Usage & Frames:* 'Play football / games', 'Play the guitar / piano', 'Play a role in a film'.
  • *Useful Phrases:* 'play sports', 'play an instrument', 'play a key role'.

**9. Agree / Disagree:** Consensus and opinion.
  • *Usage & Frames:* 'I agree with you', 'We agree on the plan', 'I disagree'.
  • *Useful Phrases:* 'totally agree', 'agree to differ', 'respectfully disagree'.

**10. Send / Get:** Transmitting and receiving.
  • *Usage & Frames:* 'Send a text message', 'I get an email', 'Get home at 6 PM'.
  • *Useful Phrases:* 'send an email', 'get back', 'get to the station'.

blocks.text: The memory map: ten verbs, five functions
blocks.say: The memory map: ten verbs, five functions

blocks.text: Instead of learning ten verbs one after another, sort them by function. When you want to say something, first ask: <mark class="hl-handwritten">am I shopping, thinking, feeling, connecting, or communicating?</mark> The verb comes almost by itself.
blocks.say: Instead of learning ten verbs one after another, sort them by function. When you want to say something, first ask: am I shopping, thinking, feeling, connecting, or communicating? The verb comes almost by itself.

items: **Shopping & resources:** choose / buy / pay, spend / waste. Money, time and choices.
**Thinking & deciding:** remember / forget, decide, agree / disagree. Memory, decisions and opinions.
**Feeling & meeting:** feel, meet. Your inner state and other people.
**Text & messages:** write / read / type, send / get. Words that travel.
**Free time:** play. Games, sport, music and roles.
blocks.say: Shopping & resources: choose / buy / pay, spend / waste. Money, time and choices. Thinking & deciding: remember / forget, decide, agree / disagree. Memory, decisions and opinions. Feeling & meeting: feel, meet. Your inner state and other people. Text & messages: write / read / type, send / get. Words that travel. Free time: play. Games, sport, music and roles.
The 10 Core Verbs in Depth (Part 3)
1. Choose / Buy / Pay

blocks.text: These three verbs follow one little story: you **choose** something, you **buy** it, and you **pay** for it. Choose is about a decision between options. Buy is about getting something in exchange for money. Pay is about handing over the money, and it behaves differently from the other two: you pay *for* a thing, but you pay a *person* or pay *by* card.
blocks.say: These three verbs follow one little story: you choose something, you buy it, and you pay for it. Choose is about a decision between options. Buy is about getting something in exchange for money. Pay is about handing over the money, and it behaves differently from the other two: you pay for a thing, but you pay a person or pay by card.

items: **Choosing:** 'choose a book', 'choose between two options', 'choose a colour'.
**Buying:** 'buy groceries', 'buy a ticket online', 'buy a present for a friend'.
**Paying:** 'pay by card', 'pay for dinner', 'pay the rent', and the fixed phrase 'pay attention'.
blocks.say: Choosing: 'choose a book', 'choose between two options', 'choose a colour'. Buying: 'buy groceries', 'buy a ticket online', 'buy a present for a friend'. Paying: 'pay by card', 'pay for dinner', 'pay the rent', and the fixed phrase 'pay attention'.
Say aloud

blocks.targetText: It is hard to choose between the red bag and the black bag.
blocks.gloss: Choose between + two things. The verb is irregular: choose, chose, chosen.
blocks.context: You are shopping with a friend.
blocks.say: It is hard to choose between the red bag and the black bag.

blocks.targetText: I bought a train ticket online, and I paid by card.
blocks.gloss: Buy and pay in one sentence: 'bought' is irregular, 'paid' is irregular too.
blocks.context: You explain how you organised a trip.
blocks.say: I bought a train ticket online, and I paid by card.

blocks.targetText: Mini-dialogue: A: Are you ready to order? B: Yes, I'll choose the soup. A: Do you want to pay now or later? B: I'll pay now. Can I pay by card?
blocks.gloss: Play both roles aloud, then swap.
blocks.context: A short exchange to rehearse with a partner or in front of the mirror.
blocks.say: Mini-dialogue: A: Are you ready to order? B: Yes, I'll choose the soup. A: Do you want to pay now or later? B: I'll pay now. Can I pay by card?

blocks.title: Pay for or pay to
blocks.why: In many languages the money goes straight onto the object. In English the thing you buy needs 'for'.
blocks.rule: **Pay for** + thing. **Pay** + person (no 'for'): 'I paid the waiter'. **Pay by** + card or cash.
blocks.say: Pay for or pay to. Not quite: 'I paid the coffee.' Say this instead: 'I paid for the coffee.' In many languages the money goes straight onto the object. In English the thing you buy needs 'for'. Pay for + thing. Pay + person (no 'for'): 'I paid the waiter'. Pay by + card or cash.

blocks.question: I will ___ for the pizza, you paid last time.
blocks.explanation: We 'pay for' a thing. 'Buy for the pizza' is not possible.
blocks.say: I will ___ for the pizza, you paid last time.
2. Remember / Forget

blocks.text: Memory verbs are short but tricky. **Remember** means that something is in your mind, or that you do not forget to do something. **Forget** means it left your mind. Both can be followed by a noun, by 'to + verb' or by '-ing', and the meaning changes: 'remember to lock the door' is a task for the future, 'remember locking the door' is a memory of the past.
blocks.say: Memory verbs are short but tricky. Remember means that something is in your mind, or that you do not forget to do something. Forget means it left your mind. Both can be followed by a noun, by 'to + verb' or by '-ing', and the meaning changes: 'remember to lock the door' is a task for the future, 'remember locking the door' is a memory of the past.

items: **Names and facts:** 'remember a name', 'remember a phone number', 'I can't remember the word'.
**Tasks:** 'remember to buy milk', 'don't forget to send the email'.
**Objects:** 'I forgot my password', 'she forgot her bag on the train'.
blocks.say: Names and facts: 'remember a name', 'remember a phone number', 'I can't remember the word'. Tasks: 'remember to buy milk', 'don't forget to send the email'. Objects: 'I forgot my password', 'she forgot her bag on the train'.
Say aloud

blocks.targetText: I remember your name, but I forgot your phone number.
blocks.gloss: Both verbs take a direct object, with no preposition.
blocks.context: You meet a friend after a long time.
blocks.say: I remember your name, but I forgot your phone number.

blocks.targetText: Remember to bring your passport tomorrow.
blocks.gloss: Remember to + verb = do not forget a future task.
blocks.context: You give advice before a trip.
blocks.say: Remember to bring your passport tomorrow.

blocks.targetText: Mini-dialogue: A: Did you remember the tickets? B: Oh no, I forgot them at home! A: Don't worry. Do you remember the password for the app? B: Yes, I remember it. I can show the ticket on my phone.
blocks.gloss: Play both roles aloud, then swap.
blocks.context: A short exchange to rehearse with a partner or in front of the mirror.
blocks.say: Mini-dialogue: A: Did you remember the tickets? B: Oh no, I forgot them at home! A: Don't worry. Do you remember the password for the app? B: Yes, I remember it. I can show the ticket on my phone.

blocks.title: Forget or leave
blocks.right: 'I left my phone at home.' (or 'I forgot my phone.')
blocks.why: Many languages use one verb for 'forget' and 'leave behind'. English says 'forget' when you do not remember, and 'leave' when you name the place.
blocks.rule: **Forget** + thing (no place). **Leave** + thing + place: 'I left my keys on the table'.
examples: She left her bag in the taxi.
He forgot to lock the door.
blocks.say: Forget or leave. Not quite: 'I forgot my phone at home.' Say this instead: 'I left my phone at home.' (or 'I forgot my phone.') Many languages use one verb for 'forget' and 'leave behind'. English says 'forget' when you do not remember, and 'leave' when you name the place. Forget + thing (no place). Leave + thing + place: 'I left my keys on the table'.

blocks.question: Please ___ to turn off the lights.
blocks.explanation: After 'please' we use the base form: 'remember to turn off the lights'.
blocks.say: Please ___ to turn off the lights.
3. Feel

blocks.text: **Feel** is one of the most useful verbs for talking about yourself. It describes how your body or mind is right now. After 'feel' we normally use an adjective, not an adverb: 'I feel happy', 'I feel tired', 'I feel cold'. It is a state, so we use the simple present for it: 'I feel better today'.
blocks.say: Feel is one of the most useful verbs for talking about yourself. It describes how your body or mind is right now. After 'feel' we normally use an adjective, not an adverb: 'I feel happy', 'I feel tired', 'I feel cold'. It is a state, so we use the simple present for it: 'I feel better today'.

items: **Body:** 'feel cold', 'feel hungry', 'feel sick', 'feel tired'.
**Emotions:** 'feel happy', 'feel nervous', 'feel proud', 'feel lonely'.
**Wanting:** 'feel like + noun / -ing': 'I feel like a coffee', 'I feel like going out'.
blocks.say: Body: 'feel cold', 'feel hungry', 'feel sick', 'feel tired'. Emotions: 'feel happy', 'feel nervous', 'feel proud', 'feel lonely'. Wanting: 'feel like + noun / -ing': 'I feel like a coffee', 'I feel like going out'.
Say aloud

blocks.targetText: I feel tired today, but I feel much better after lunch.
blocks.gloss: Feel + adjective. The past form of feel is 'felt'.
blocks.context: You answer a colleague who asks about your day.
blocks.say: I feel tired today, but I feel much better after lunch.

blocks.targetText: Do you feel like going for a walk?
blocks.gloss: Feel like + -ing = would you like to?
blocks.context: You invite a friend.
blocks.say: Do you feel like going for a walk?

blocks.targetText: Mini-dialogue: A: How do you feel? B: I feel a bit sick. A: Do you feel hot or cold? B: I feel cold. A: Let's go home. You need to rest.
blocks.gloss: Play both roles aloud, then swap.
blocks.context: A short exchange to rehearse with a partner or in front of the mirror.
blocks.say: Mini-dialogue: A: How do you feel? B: I feel a bit sick. A: Do you feel hot or cold? B: I feel cold. A: Let's go home. You need to rest.

blocks.title: Feel good or feel well
blocks.why: Learners add -ly to every adjective after a verb. But 'feel' links you to a state, so it takes an adjective, not an adverb.
blocks.rule: **Feel** + adjective: bad, good, tired, happy. 'Well' is also fine for health: 'I don't feel well'.
blocks.say: Feel good or feel well. Not quite: 'I feel badly today.' Say this instead: 'I feel bad today.' Learners add -ly to every adjective after a verb. But 'feel' links you to a state, so it takes an adjective, not an adverb. Feel + adjective: bad, good, tired, happy. 'Well' is also fine for health: 'I don't feel well'.

blocks.question: How do you ___ today?
blocks.explanation: After 'do you', we use the base form: 'How do you feel?'
blocks.say: How do you ___ today?
4. Meet

blocks.text: **Meet** is used when two people come together, by plan or by chance. It is also the verb of first introductions: 'Nice to meet you!'. It takes a direct object, so we say 'I meet my friend', not 'I meet with my friend' in simple situations (the 'with' version exists in American English for formal meetings).
blocks.say: Meet is used when two people come together, by plan or by chance. It is also the verb of first introductions: 'Nice to meet you!'. It takes a direct object, so we say 'I meet my friend', not 'I meet with my friend' in simple situations (the 'with' version exists in American English for formal meetings).

rows: She meets her teacher at nine.
I have a meeting at ten.

items: **First time:** 'Nice to meet you', 'Pleased to meet you', 'Meet my friend Sara'.
**Arrangements:** 'Let's meet at 5 PM', 'meet outside the cinema', 'meet up on Saturday'.
**Chance:** 'I met an old friend in the street', 'meet new people'.
blocks.say: First time: 'Nice to meet you', 'Pleased to meet you', 'Meet my friend Sara'. Arrangements: 'Let's meet at 5 PM', 'meet outside the cinema', 'meet up on Saturday'. Chance: 'I met an old friend in the street', 'meet new people'.
Say aloud

blocks.targetText: Nice to meet you. I'm Tom, and this is my sister.
blocks.gloss: A polite fixed phrase for a first meeting.
blocks.context: You are introduced at a party.
blocks.say: Nice to meet you. I'm Tom, and this is my sister.

blocks.targetText: Let's meet at the station at half past six.
blocks.gloss: Let's meet + place + time.
blocks.context: You make a plan with a friend.
blocks.say: Let's meet at the station at half past six.

blocks.targetText: Mini-dialogue: A: Hi, have we met before? B: I don't think so. I'm Maria. A: Nice to meet you, Maria. I'm Leo. Let's meet for coffee next week! B: Great idea.
blocks.gloss: Play both roles aloud, then swap.
blocks.context: A short exchange to rehearse with a partner or in front of the mirror.
blocks.say: Mini-dialogue: A: Hi, have we met before? B: I don't think so. I'm Maria. A: Nice to meet you, Maria. I'm Leo. Let's meet for coffee next week! B: Great idea.

blocks.title: Meet or know
blocks.right: 'I have known her for five years.'
blocks.why: In many languages the verb for 'meet' also works for 'know someone'. In English, 'meet' is a moment, not a long state.
blocks.rule: **Meet** = the first time or an event. **Know** = a long relationship: 'I have known her for years'.
blocks.say: Meet or know. Not quite: 'I met her for five years.' Say this instead: 'I have known her for five years.' In many languages the verb for 'meet' also works for 'know someone'. In English, 'meet' is a moment, not a long state. Meet = the first time or an event. Know = a long relationship: 'I have known her for years'.

blocks.question: It was nice to ___ you.
blocks.explanation: At a first encounter we say 'nice to meet you'. 'Nice to know you' is not the usual phrase.
blocks.say: It was nice to ___ you.

blocks.title: First meetings in English
blocks.content: A handshake and a smile are the usual greeting at a first meeting, with 'Nice to meet you' as the answer from both people. Hugs and kisses on the cheek are less common between new acquaintances than in many countries. After the first meeting, 'Good to see you' is more natural than 'Nice to meet you'. Small talk about the weather, the journey or the weekend is a friendly way to start.
blocks.say: First meetings in English. A handshake and a smile are the usual greeting at a first meeting, with 'Nice to meet you' as the answer from both people. Hugs and kisses on the cheek are less common between new acquaintances than in many countries. After the first meeting, 'Good to see you' is more natural than 'Nice to meet you'. Small talk about the weather, the journey or the weekend is a friendly way to start.
5. Decide

blocks.text: **Decide** is about reaching a decision: you think, then you choose. It can be followed by 'to + verb' ('I decide to stay'), by 'on' + a thing ('decide on a hotel') or used alone ('I can't decide'). Remember the important note: we do not 'decide a problem' in English. A problem is **solved**. A decision is **made**.
blocks.say: Decide is about reaching a decision: you think, then you choose. It can be followed by 'to + verb' ('I decide to stay'), by 'on' + a thing ('decide on a hotel') or used alone ('I can't decide'). Remember the important note: we do not 'decide a problem' in English. A problem is solved. A decision is made.

items: **To do something:** 'decide to stay', 'decide to learn English'.
**To choose a thing:** 'decide on a date', 'decide on a name'.
**Common phrases:** 'decide quickly', 'hard to decide', 'make up your mind', 'I haven't decided yet'.
blocks.say: To do something: 'decide to stay', 'decide to learn English'. To choose a thing: 'decide on a date', 'decide on a name'. Common phrases: 'decide quickly', 'hard to decide', 'make up your mind', 'I haven't decided yet'.
Say aloud

blocks.targetText: I decided to learn English last year.
blocks.gloss: Decide + to + verb.
blocks.context: You tell your story at a language school.
blocks.say: I decided to learn English last year.

blocks.targetText: We need to decide on a restaurant for Friday.
blocks.gloss: Decide on = choose after thinking.
blocks.context: You plan a group dinner.
blocks.say: We need to decide on a restaurant for Friday.

blocks.targetText: Mini-dialogue: A: Have you decided? B: Not yet. I can't decide between the pizza and the pasta. A: Make up your mind! B: OK, I decide on the pasta.
blocks.gloss: Play both roles aloud, then swap.
blocks.context: A short exchange to rehearse with a partner or in front of the mirror.
blocks.say: Mini-dialogue: A: Have you decided? B: Not yet. I can't decide between the pizza and the pasta. A: Make up your mind! B: OK, I decide on the pasta.

blocks.title: Decide a problem
blocks.why: The verb 'decide' in many languages (for example Russian 'решать') also means 'solve'. English splits the meanings.
blocks.rule: **Solve** a problem or a puzzle. **Decide** to do something. **Make** a decision.
blocks.say: Decide a problem. Not quite: 'We must decide this problem.' Say this instead: 'We must solve this problem.' The verb 'decide' in many languages (for example Russian 'решать') also means 'solve'. English splits the meanings. Solve a problem or a puzzle. Decide to do something. Make a decision.

blocks.question: It is hard to ___ between two jobs.
blocks.explanation: We decide between choices. We solve problems.
blocks.say: It is hard to ___ between two jobs.
6. Write / Read / Type

blocks.text: Three verbs of text: **write** (create words by hand or on screen), **read** (take in the words) and **type** (write with a keyboard). Read is special in speaking: the base form is /riːd/, but the past and the participle are spelled the same and pronounced /rɛd/. This is a small trap, and one you can learn in one minute.
blocks.say: Three verbs of text: write (create words by hand or on screen), read (take in the words) and type (write with a keyboard). Read is special in speaking: the base form is /riːd/, but the past and the participle are spelled the same and pronounced /rɛd/. This is a small trap, and one you can learn in one minute.

rows: I read the news every day.

items: **Writing:** 'write an email', 'write a story', 'write down your address'.
**Reading:** 'read a book', 'read aloud', 'read the instructions'.
**Typing:** 'type a message', 'type fast', 'type your password'.
blocks.say: Writing: 'write an email', 'write a story', 'write down your address'. Reading: 'read a book', 'read aloud', 'read the instructions'. Typing: 'type a message', 'type fast', 'type your password'.
Say aloud

blocks.targetText: I write an email to my teacher every Monday.
blocks.gloss: Write + object. Past form: wrote.
blocks.context: You describe your weekly routine.
blocks.say: I write an email to my teacher every Monday.

blocks.targetText: Please read the text aloud and type the answer.
blocks.gloss: Two imperatives in a classroom.
blocks.context: Your teacher gives instructions.
blocks.say: Please read the text aloud and type the answer.

blocks.targetText: Mini-dialogue: A: What are you doing? B: I'm writing a message. A: Can you read it to me? B: Sure. Wait, I need to type one more line.
blocks.gloss: Play both roles aloud, then swap.
blocks.context: A short exchange to rehearse with a partner or in front of the mirror.
blocks.say: Mini-dialogue: A: What are you doing? B: I'm writing a message. A: Can you read it to me? B: Sure. Wait, I need to type one more line.

blocks.title: Read in the past
blocks.why: Learners add -ed to every past verb. 'Read' is irregular: the spelling does not change, only the sound.
blocks.rule: **Read** (/riːd/) in the present, **read** (/rɛd/) in the past. Write: wrote, written.
blocks.say: Read in the past. Not quite: 'Yesterday I readed a good book.' Say this instead: 'Yesterday I read a good book.' Learners add -ed to every past verb. 'Read' is irregular: the spelling does not change, only the sound. Read (/riːd/) in the present, read (/rɛd/) in the past. Write: wrote, written.

blocks.question: Yesterday I ___ a letter to my aunt.
blocks.explanation: Simple past of write is 'wrote'. 'Written' needs 'have'.
blocks.say: Yesterday I ___ a letter to my aunt.
7. Spend / Waste

blocks.text: **Spend** and **waste** both use up a resource: money, time or energy. The difference is judgement. **Spend** is neutral or positive ('I spend time with my family'). **Waste** is negative: you use too much, or you use it badly. The preposition is important: you spend money **on** something, and you spend time **with** a person or **doing** something.
blocks.say: Spend and waste both use up a resource: money, time or energy. The difference is judgement. Spend is neutral or positive ('I spend time with my family'). Waste is negative: you use too much, or you use it badly. The preposition is important: you spend money on something, and you spend time with a person or doing something.

rows: I spent an hour on it.

items: **Money:** 'spend money on books', 'spend too much', 'spend less'.
**Time:** 'spend time with family', 'spend a week in Italy', 'spend an hour studying'.
**Waste:** 'waste energy', 'waste water', 'waste food', 'it's a waste of time'.
blocks.say: Money: 'spend money on books', 'spend too much', 'spend less'. Time: 'spend time with family', 'spend a week in Italy', 'spend an hour studying'. Waste: 'waste energy', 'waste water', 'waste food', 'it's a waste of time'.
Say aloud

blocks.targetText: I spend a lot of money on books and coffee.
blocks.gloss: Spend + money + on + thing.
blocks.context: You talk about your habits.
blocks.say: I spend a lot of money on books and coffee.

blocks.targetText: We spent the weekend with my grandparents.
blocks.gloss: Spend + time + with + people.
blocks.context: You tell a friend about your weekend.
blocks.say: We spent the weekend with my grandparents.

blocks.targetText: Mini-dialogue: A: Why are you leaving the lights on? B: Oh, sorry! A: Don't waste energy. B: You're right. How much did you spend on the new lamp? A: Not much. I spent ten euros.
blocks.gloss: Play both roles aloud, then swap.
blocks.context: A short exchange to rehearse with a partner or in front of the mirror.
blocks.say: Mini-dialogue: A: Why are you leaving the lights on? B: Oh, sorry! A: Don't waste energy. B: You're right. How much did you spend on the new lamp? A: Not much. I spent ten euros.

blocks.title: Spend a holiday or pass
blocks.why: Many languages say 'pass the time'. In English, we **spend** time, and 'pass' is mostly for the exam or the salt.
blocks.rule: **Spend** time or money. **Pass** an exam or a person in the street. **Take** a trip.
blocks.say: Spend a holiday or pass. Not quite: 'I passed the weekend at home.' Say this instead: 'I spent the weekend at home.' Many languages say 'pass the time'. In English, we spend time, and 'pass' is mostly for the exam or the salt. Spend time or money. Pass an exam or a person in the street. Take a trip.

blocks.question: Please don't ___ water when you wash the dishes.
blocks.explanation: Waste = use too much. We 'waste water', not 'spend water'.
blocks.say: Please don't ___ water when you wash the dishes.

blocks.title: Time is money
blocks.content: English has many sayings that compare time to money: 'spend time', 'save time', 'waste time', 'invest time'. This shows how English speakers often think about time, as something valuable you can run out of. A polite way to say you are short of time is 'I'm afraid I don't have much time', and an apology for taking someone's time is 'Sorry to waste your time'.
blocks.say: Time is money. English has many sayings that compare time to money: 'spend time', 'save time', 'waste time', 'invest time'. This shows how English speakers often think about time, as something valuable you can run out of. A polite way to say you are short of time is 'I'm afraid I don't have much time', and an apology for taking someone's time is 'Sorry to waste your time'.
8. Play (all variations)

blocks.text: **Play** has several faces, and each one has its own little rule. With sports and games, there is no article: 'play football', 'play chess'. With musical instruments, we use 'the': 'play the guitar'. In theatre and film, we play a role or a part. And with children, play is simply fun: 'the kids play in the park'.
blocks.say: Play has several faces, and each one has its own little rule. With sports and games, there is no article: 'play football', 'play chess'. With musical instruments, we use 'the': 'play the guitar'. In theatre and film, we play a role or a part. And with children, play is simply fun: 'the kids play in the park'.

rows: He plays a doctor in the film.

items: **Sports and games:** 'play football', 'play cards', 'play video games'.
**Music:** 'play the guitar', 'play a song', 'play music'.
**Roles and fixed phrases:** 'play a key role', 'play a trick on someone', 'play it safe'.
blocks.say: Sports and games: 'play football', 'play cards', 'play video games'. Music: 'play the guitar', 'play a song', 'play music'. Roles and fixed phrases: 'play a key role', 'play a trick on someone', 'play it safe'.
Say aloud

blocks.targetText: I play football on Sundays and my brother plays the guitar.
blocks.gloss: Sport with no article; instrument with 'the'.
blocks.context: You describe your family hobbies.
blocks.say: I play football on Sundays and my brother plays the guitar.

blocks.targetText: Can you play this song again? I love it.
blocks.gloss: Play also works for music from a device.
blocks.context: You are with friends at home.
blocks.say: Can you play this song again? I love it.

blocks.targetText: Mini-dialogue: A: Do you play any sports? B: I play basketball. And you? A: I play the violin, but I don't play sports. B: Let's play a game tonight!
blocks.gloss: Play both roles aloud, then swap.
blocks.context: A short exchange to rehearse with a partner or in front of the mirror.
blocks.say: Mini-dialogue: A: Do you play any sports? B: I play basketball. And you? A: I play the violin, but I don't play sports. B: Let's play a game tonight!

blocks.title: Play the football
blocks.why: Learners think of the article from their own language. In English, sports do not take 'the' after play.
blocks.rule: **Play** + sport (no article). **Play the** + instrument. **Go** + -ing for some activities: 'go swimming'.
blocks.say: Play the football. Not quite: 'I play the football.' Say this instead: 'I play football.' Learners think of the article from their own language. In English, sports do not take 'the' after play. Play + sport (no article). Play the + instrument. Go + -ing for some activities: 'go swimming'.

blocks.question: My sister ___ the piano very well.
blocks.say: My sister ___ the piano very well.
9. Agree / Disagree

blocks.text: Opinions need two verbs: **agree** and **disagree**. They usually take the preposition **with** for a person ('I agree with you') and **on** or **about** for a topic ('we agree on the plan'). Do not say 'I am agree', because 'agree' is already a verb in English. It is not an adjective.
blocks.say: Opinions need two verbs: agree and disagree. They usually take the preposition with for a person ('I agree with you') and on or about for a topic ('we agree on the plan'). Do not say 'I am agree', because 'agree' is already a verb in English. It is not an adjective.

rows: They are agreeing on a price.

items: **With a person:** 'I agree with you', 'I disagree with her'.
**On a plan:** 'we agree on the plan', 'agree on a price'.
**Common phrases:** 'totally agree', 'agree to differ', 'respectfully disagree'.
blocks.say: With a person: 'I agree with you', 'I disagree with her'. On a plan: 'we agree on the plan', 'agree on a price'. Common phrases: 'totally agree', 'agree to differ', 'respectfully disagree'.
Say aloud

blocks.targetText: I agree with you, but I disagree with the price.
blocks.gloss: Agree with + person. Disagree with + thing.
blocks.context: You discuss a purchase with a friend.
blocks.say: I agree with you, but I disagree with the price.

blocks.targetText: We agreed to meet at six.
blocks.gloss: Agree to + verb = accept a plan.
blocks.context: You report an arrangement.
blocks.say: We agreed to meet at six.

blocks.targetText: Mini-dialogue: A: I think the film was great. B: I disagree. I thought it was too long. A: OK, let's agree to differ! B: Fine. Do you agree on pizza for dinner? A: Totally.
blocks.gloss: Play both roles aloud, then swap.
blocks.context: A short exchange to rehearse with a partner or in front of the mirror.
blocks.say: Mini-dialogue: A: I think the film was great. B: I disagree. I thought it was too long. A: OK, let's agree to differ! B: Fine. Do you agree on pizza for dinner? A: Totally.

blocks.title: I am agree
blocks.why: In several languages the expression is 'to be in agreement' or 'to be agree', so learners copy the structure with 'be'.
blocks.rule: **Agree** is a normal verb: 'I agree', 'he agrees'. Never use 'am / is / are' before it.
blocks.say: I am agree. Not quite: 'I am agree with you.' Say this instead: 'I agree with you.' In several languages the expression is 'to be in agreement' or 'to be agree', so learners copy the structure with 'be'. Agree is a normal verb: 'I agree', 'he agrees'. Never use 'am / is / are' before it.

blocks.question: I don't ___ with you. I think it is a bad idea.
blocks.say: I don't ___ with you. I think it is a bad idea.

blocks.title: Disagreeing politely
blocks.content: In English, a direct 'No, you're wrong' can sound rude. Native speakers usually soften a disagreement: 'I see what you mean, but...', 'I'm not sure I agree', 'That's a good point, however...'. In a meeting, these phrases keep the conversation friendly. Using 'respectfully' or 'with respect' before 'disagree' shows politeness and is common in formal discussions.
blocks.say: Disagreeing politely. In English, a direct 'No, you're wrong' can sound rude. Native speakers usually soften a disagreement: 'I see what you mean, but...', 'I'm not sure I agree', 'That's a good point, however...'. In a meeting, these phrases keep the conversation friendly. Using 'respectfully' or 'with respect' before 'disagree' shows politeness and is common in formal discussions.
10. Send / Get

blocks.text: **Send** goes away from you: you send a message, a parcel, a photo. **Get** comes to you: you get an email, a gift, a message. Get is one of the most frequent verbs in English and has many meanings: receive, become, arrive, buy, understand. At A0–A2 level, focus on three: receive, arrive and become.
blocks.say: Send goes away from you: you send a message, a parcel, a photo. Get comes to you: you get an email, a gift, a message. Get is one of the most frequent verbs in English and has many meanings: receive, become, arrive, buy, understand. At A0–A2 level, focus on three: receive, arrive and become.

rows: I get ten emails a day.

items: **Sending:** 'send a text message', 'send an email', 'send a letter', 'send money'.
**Receiving:** 'I get an email', 'get a message', 'get a present'.
**Arriving and becoming:** 'get home at 6 PM', 'get to the station', 'get back', 'get tired'.
blocks.say: Sending: 'send a text message', 'send an email', 'send a letter', 'send money'. Receiving: 'I get an email', 'get a message', 'get a present'. Arriving and becoming: 'get home at 6 PM', 'get to the station', 'get back', 'get tired'.
Say aloud

blocks.targetText: I sent you an email this morning. Did you get it?
blocks.gloss: Send + person + thing. Get = receive.
blocks.context: You check with a colleague.
blocks.say: I sent you an email this morning. Did you get it?

blocks.targetText: I usually get home at six, and I get tired in the evening.
blocks.gloss: Get + place = arrive. Get + adjective = become.
blocks.context: You talk about your day.
blocks.say: I usually get home at six, and I get tired in the evening.

blocks.targetText: Mini-dialogue: A: Did you send the photos? B: Yes, I sent them an hour ago. A: I didn't get them. B: Let me send them again. A: Thanks. When do you get home? B: At seven.
blocks.gloss: Play both roles aloud, then swap.
blocks.context: A short exchange to rehearse with a partner or in front of the mirror.
blocks.say: Mini-dialogue: A: Did you send the photos? B: Yes, I sent them an hour ago. A: I didn't get them. B: Let me send them again. A: Thanks. When do you get home? B: At seven.

blocks.title: Send or get a letter
blocks.wrong: 'I sent a letter from my friend.'
blocks.right: 'I got a letter from my friend.'
blocks.why: In many languages, one verb can mean both 'send' and 'receive' depending on context. In English, the direction is built into the verb.
blocks.rule: **Send** = away from you. **Get / receive** = towards you. Never use 'send' for something that arrives.
examples: I sent a card to Anna.
She got a card from Tom.
blocks.say: Send or get a letter. Not quite: 'I sent a letter from my friend.' Say this instead: 'I got a letter from my friend.' In many languages, one verb can mean both 'send' and 'receive' depending on context. In English, the direction is built into the verb. Send = away from you. Get / receive = towards you. Never use 'send' for something that arrives.

blocks.question: I didn't ___ your message. Can you send it again?
blocks.explanation: 'Get' = receive. After 'didn't' use the base form: 'didn't get'.
blocks.say: I didn't ___ your message. Can you send it again?

blocks.title: Texts, emails and etiquette
blocks.content: In English-speaking countries, it is common to reply to a message within a day, and to send a short 'thank you' after a gift or a favour. In work emails, a polite start ('Hi Anna,', 'Dear Mr Brown,') and an ending ('Best regards', 'Kind regards') are standard. Use 'Could you send me...?' instead of 'Send me...' to sound polite.
blocks.say: Texts, emails and etiquette. In English-speaking countries, it is common to reply to a message within a day, and to send a short 'thank you' after a gift or a favour. In work emails, a polite start ('Hi Anna,', 'Dear Mr Brown,') and an ending ('Best regards', 'Kind regards') are standard. Use 'Could you send me...?' instead of 'Send me...' to sound polite.

blocks.say: Your 5-minute speaking routine

blocks.text: Five minutes a day, out loud, beat an hour of silent reading on Sunday. Here is a simple plan to repeat for one week: <mark class="hl-handwritten">one minute per step, no more</mark>.
blocks.say: Five minutes a day, out loud, beat an hour of silent reading on Sunday. Here is a simple plan to repeat for one week: one minute per step, no more.

items: **Minute 1, warm-up:** say the three forms of buy, pay, forget, feel, meet, write, spend and send without looking at the tables.
**Minute 2, three verbs, three sentences:** choose three verbs and say one true sentence about your life for each: 'I spend...', 'I feel...', 'I agree with...'.
**Minute 3, mistake hunt:** reread one 'Not quite' card and say the correct sentence three times, changing the subject each time.
**Minute 4, mini-dialogue:** play both roles of a dialogue with 'Can I pay by card?', 'Do you remember...?', 'Did you get my message?', and record yourself on your phone.
**Minute 5, replay:** listen to the recording and pick one sentence to keep for tomorrow. Write it on a note near your desk.

Your one-week action plan

blocks.text: Do not try to learn all ten verbs in one day. Give each day a small mission and keep it real: use your own life, your own money, your own friends.
blocks.say: Do not try to learn all ten verbs in one day. Give each day a small mission and keep it real: use your own life, your own money, your own friends.

items: **Day 1:** order or buy something and say 'I choose...', 'I pay by card' aloud, even at home.
**Day 2:** write three notes with 'remember to' and 'don't forget to' and stick them on your door.
**Day 3:** tell someone how you feel, in three different words: 'I feel tired, nervous, happy.'
**Day 4:** meet someone, in person or online, and say 'Nice to meet you' and one follow-up question.
**Day 5:** read ten lines aloud, write five lines about them, and type one line on your phone.
**Day 6:** check your week: what did you spend money and time on? Say it with 'spend... on'.
**Day 7:** send a short message in English to a friend, and agree or disagree with their answer politely.
